transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

A failing battery can trip its protection after a few seconds, then behave normally again on another occasion. The other realistic possibility is the powered floorhead/brush-bar drawing too much current. 1. Fully charge it, use normal power rather than Max/Boost, and wipe the charging/battery contacts with a clean dry cloth.
2. With it switched off first, remove the wand and floorhead. Then run the main unit briefly with no attachments. If it runs steadily this way but cuts out with the head fitted, inspect the roller for hair/thread and make sure it turns freely; the issue is likely in the floorhead rather than the battery.
3. If it still stops after 5–10 seconds with no attachments, watch for any flashing lights when it stops. That pattern would strongly support the battery/protection system; if there are no lights and it becomes hot or smells burnt, internal motor/electronics diagnosis is an engineer job. Do not buy a battery just yet: the no-attachment test is the useful separator.

Ok. Handheld with no tool it still cuts out sometimes, just less often. On Max it nearly always stops within a few seconds. Sometimes the blue lights flash a few times when it stops, sometimes nothing. The battery isn't swollen or hot and there's no smell. So is it the battery?

Yes — the battery is now the leading suspect, though not proven enough to buy one yet. Cutting out much more readily on Max, while it can still happen with the wand and head removed, is the usual pattern of a tired battery whose protection trips when demand is high. Being neither hot nor swollen does not rule that out. The blue flashes also point to a protection fault, but the exact number matters: it can distinguish battery protection from another fault. 1. Fully charge it, then use normal power with no attachment fitted. When it stops, count the blue flashes exactly before they go out. That is the most useful confirmation.
2. Make sure the washed filter was allowed to dry completely for at least 24 hours before use. A damp filter can still restrict airflow and cause cut-outs, although your no-attachment/Max result makes the battery more likely. If it cuts out within seconds on normal power, fully charged and bare, with a repeatable flash pattern, the battery is the likely replaceable component. If the lights are inconsistent or it begins cutting out even when cool and freshly charged, the motor/control electronics become more likely and an engineer repair assessment is the better route.

I did wash the filter and let it dry for 48 hours, so that's covered. The blue lights sometimes flash 3 times, sometimes nothing. It's also been left on the charger permanently, if that matters. Is the battery worth the £60+ then?

Switch it off and unplug it (or take the battery off) first. Probably yes — a battery is the most likely £60+ repair, but I would not spend the money until one final, simple test suggests it. The strongest evidence is that it cuts out even as a bare handheld and does so much more readily on Max. Clean, dry filters and no blockage make an airflow thermal cut-out less likely. A five-year-old battery can lose its ability to supply high current, so its protection shuts it down. Leaving it docked permanently is not usually an immediate problem because the charger manages charging, but age and time spent at high charge can still contribute to battery wear. The inconsistent three blue flashes do not prove a specific Dyson fault code, so I would not use that alone to justify a battery. 1. Give it a full charge, then remove it from the charger and run it on normal power with no wand or tool attached. Time it from pressing the trigger to cut-out. - If it stops within seconds or a minute or two, the battery is strongly indicated and a replacement is likely to be worthwhile. - If it runs steadily bare on normal power but fails only with the floorhead, the floorhead/brush-bar load is the more likely issue. - If a replacement battery would not cure it, the remaining possibility is the motor/control electronics; that is usually an engineer-level repair and is less attractive financially on a five-year-old cordless vacuum. Avoid very cheap unbranded batteries: quality and protection circuitry vary considerably. If the timed bare-handheld test is short, a reputable compatible or genuine battery is a reasonable repair; if it runs normally, do not buy the battery yet.
Ok, I'll do the full charge and the timed bare handheld test on normal power. I don't have a spare battery to swap in, so that's as far as I can test it. I'll come back with how long it runs.

That is the right test, and no spare battery is needed for it to be useful. Please time the bare handheld run on normal power after the full charge and report the approximate runtime and whether it simply stops or flashes blue lights. A short, repeatable run strongly supports the battery; a steady normal run would shift suspicion back towards the floorhead or an intermittent internal control fault.
Ok, will do. Anything else I should look out for while I run it, or just time it and note the lights?

Mainly time it and note the lights. Also note these two details, as they help separate a battery issue from a motor/control fault: 1. Does it stop abruptly as if the trigger was released, or does it pulse/surge first? An abrupt stop, especially with blue flashes, favours battery protection. Pulsing tends more towards an airflow restriction.
2. Is the motor body noticeably hot by the time it stops? A cool-to-warm body with a very short run still favours the battery; significant heat after only a short bare-handheld run would make the motor or electronics more concerning. Do not keep repeatedly restarting it after a cut-out. Stop the test if it becomes hot, smells unusual, or the battery changes shape. Otherwise, the runtime, stop pattern and any blue-flash count are enough for the next call on whether the battery is genuinely indicated.
Ok, thanks. From what I've seen it's a clean stop, no pulsing, and it's not been hot or smelly. I'll time it and let you know.

That clean stop, with no pulsing, overheating or unusual smell, makes an airflow/thermal cut-out less likely and keeps the battery/protection circuit as the leading cause. The timed bare-handheld run is the useful final separator. After the full charge, run it on normal power with no wand or tool and note the approximate time to cut-out plus any blue flashes. If it repeats a very short run — seconds to a minute or two — the battery will be strongly indicated. If it instead runs normally bare but fails with the floorhead attached, the floorhead/brush-bar load becomes the more likely fault. Avoid repeatedly restarting it if it cuts out; one timed run is enough.
Yes, understood, one timed run on normal power with nothing attached, and I'll note the lights. I'll report back once I've done it.

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
The battery remains the likely cause: it cuts out even as a bare handheld, is much worse on Max, and the filter/airways have been cleaned and dried. A motor or control fault is still possible, but less likely at this stage. Before buying a battery, please find the full model number from the rating label. “V” series and purple trim are not enough to identify the correct battery, as several Dyson versions look similar but use different fittings. It is usually on the main body, often beneath the bin or near the battery. If the label is awkward to reach, it can wait—do not dismantle the vacuum to get it.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
I checked the label and it says SV11. That's the full model number I can find. Does that help you pick the right battery?

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
Yes—SV11 is useful as a model-family identifier, but it is not enough for me to safely specify an exact replacement battery or fitting. Dyson made variants within that family, and battery connections can differ, so buy only through Dyson’s spares checker using the serial number as well as SV11, or have a reputable vacuum-repair shop match it. The symptom pattern still points most strongly to the battery: it cuts out with no tool fitted, yet is much more likely to stop within seconds on Max, despite the filter being properly dried and the airways checked. There is no reported overheating, smell or swelling, which is reassuring and makes an airflow thermal cut-out less likely. A genuine Dyson battery, or a reputable UK supplier’s correctly matched battery with proper protection electronics, is the sensible route. Avoid the cheapest marketplace listings. If a correctly matched replacement battery does not cure it, the remaining likely fault is the motor/control electronics; that is generally an engineer repair and may not be economical at around five years old.
